newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Santa letters from smart kids increase every year.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Santa letters from smart kids increase every year.

text.p: Out of the mouths of babes come pearls of wisdom, and children are usually savvy about what to say to Santa Claus -- but can it get them a "Tickle Me Elmo" or a "Hungry Hungry Hippo" toy?

Letters written by children to Saint Nick are growing in number every year, with more than 1 million expected to pass through U.S. post offices this year, postal service officials say. And kids are taking steps to make sure they get what they want and that Santa makes it safely to their homes.

"We get letters with coupons in them for the toys that the kids want," said Misty Sweet, a teacher who helps run a "Santa Project" at a Pittsburgh high school. The project collects letters to Santa and students answer the ones with return addresses. They also collect and distribute toys to needy children using donations from local businesses.
Sweet said students collected 3,000 letters last year and expected even more this year.

Besides sending Santa money-saving coupons, kids write letters to Mrs. Claus and Rudolph, the red-nosed reindeer. "They tell Mrs. Claus to take good care of Santa so he can 'do his job' and they tell Rudolph to make sure Santa gets to their homes safely," Sweet said. "We get letters with carrots in them so Rudolph has something to eat."
Requests to Santa range from simple to hilarious to tragic. Some children want just a few toys, "but we got one letter that had 152 toys listed," Sweet said.
KIDS ASK SANTA FOR SIBLINGS
Some children make Santa's job difficult. "We have kids who want a baby brother or sister and one little girl asked Santa to make her little brother behave better," she said.

"The last three years we've gotten a lot more needy letters," she said. "We got a letter from a child in Arizona asking Santa to put running water in his house." And children with sick parents write Santa asking him to make them well.

Sandra Harding, a spokeswoman at U.S. Postal Service headquarters in Washington, said the post office encourages children to write to Santa. "(The) number is growing every year because of the programmes we do," she said.
Letters that go through the post office do not end up in dead letter bins -- or in Manhattan court rooms, as in the classic Christmas movie "Miracle on 34th Street."

In communities from Alaska to Indiana to Virginia, and in cities including Boston, Cincinnati and New York, the postal service has programmes where volunteers answer Santa letters and help out needy families with toys, food and clothing.

New York boasts one of the the oldest Santa letter campaigns. "Operation Santa Claus" dates back more than 60 years and letters are received from around the world, Andy Sozzi, spokesman for the New York post office, said.

The public is invited to read Santa letters at post offices and people can answer as many as they want. Some also buy toys, food, blankets and clothing for needy children and adults. "We're expecting in excess of 151,000 Santa letters this year," Sozzi said.
SANTA'S MAILBOX IN FLORIDA

In Coral Gables, Florida, workers at the city's Parks & Recreation Department make sure every letter to Santa dropped in a large, shiny "Santa's Mailbox" in a park across from city hall is answered, as long as children include their return addresses and drop them in by Dec. 16. "There are so many, we have to have some leeway," a city spokeswoman said.
The Pittsburgh Zoo has a mailbox for Santa letters at its reindeer paddock to ensure that letters are taken straight to the jolly old elf by his trusty pack of four-hoofed friends.

Not every child relies on the post office, however. Four-year-old Dominic Morra said he trusted the wind to carry his four letters to Santa. "I saw more stuff I wanted so I had to write more letters," he explained, adding that he stood outside with his mom and released the letters to the wind.
Nine-year-old Terry Paul tried a different strategy. "I did it like they do it on TV," he said. "I just wished for the stuff I want instead of writing and Santa will bring it to me."

For high-tech whizzkids, there is a blizzard of ways to contact Santa on-line. Anne Bentley, spokesperson for America OnLine, said children can send electronic e-mail to Santa at the address "santaclaus @ aol.com."
"We get over 1,000 e-mails a day," she said. "Each one gets a personal reply from Santa."
